column1: Data goes missing: a forecast is late, a meter drops out, the value function has not been refreshed, the solver times out, the reserve price feed is stale.
Silent imputation makes the engine take full-confidence decisions on invented data, and the failure is invisible until Settlement.
Failing closed on anything halts the engine perpetually, because in practice something is always slightly stale, and the exceptions added in response leave no policy.
Handling degradation with if branches scattered across layers forms a state machine nobody designed and nobody can test.
Every value crossing C1 carries a value, a knowledgeTime, a provenance and a quality.
Provenance is one of Measured, Forecast, Revised, Imputed or Default.
Quality is one of Good, Degraded, Stale, Imputed or Missing.
Downstream layers do not branch on quality but map quality onto a risk multiplier that feeds the existing risk machinery.
A degraded price belief widens the CVaR confidence level and shrinks position bounds.
A stale value function attracts a staleness penalty on its terminal value.
An imputed load forecast widens the peak epigraph's safety margin.
Bad data takes the same code path with more conservative parameters rather than a different code path.
There is one code path to test, and the response to degradation is continuous and tunable rather than a cliff.
Global behaviour is a single mode computed centrally from the quality state and written to L0.
NORMAL mode triggers when all critical inputs are Good and runs the full strategy.
DEGRADED mode triggers when non-critical inputs are stale or imputed and runs the full strategy with widened risk and reduced position limits.

DEFENSIVE mode triggers when a critical input is stale, or the value function is beyond validity, or the solver hits the time limit repeatedly, and honours commitments and maintains peak protection with no new speculative exposure.
SAFE mode triggers when a critical input is missing or the commitment ledger is inconsistent, honours existing commitments only, cancels unfilled speculative orders, and holds SOC in a safe band.
HALT mode triggers when a physical constraint is violated, the state store is unreadable, or contract validation fails; it submits nothing, alerts, and requires operator acknowledgement to resume.
Mode transitions are hysteretic: entering DEFENSIVE requires N consecutive bad ticks and leaving it requires M consecutive good ones, with M greater than N.
Without hysteresis the engine flaps on a marginal feed, and the flapping is worse than either state.
Every mode transition is logged with its cause and is part of the settlement record, so a period of poor P&L can be attributed to degraded operation rather than to strategy.
Peak protection — the epigraph floor from realised peak and the qualification guard — applies in every mode including SAFE.
Losing a year of network-charge reduction because a price feed was stale is not an acceptable outcome of any degradation path.
Awarded aFRR capacity is a physical obligation.
In every mode the SOC corridor required to deliver confirmed commitments is a hard constraint, and if it cannot be met the engine goes to HALT and alerts rather than quietly under-delivering.
The fallback ladder for a single field is applied in order, stopping at the first success and recording where it stopped.
Rung 1 of the fallback ladder is the primary source, fresh.
Rung 2 of the fallback ladder is the primary source stale within maxStale, marked Stale.
Rung 3 of the fallback ladder is a secondary source, marked Degraded.
Rung 4 of the fallback ladder is model imputation by persistence, climatology or ensemble mean, marked Imputed.
Rung 5 of the fallback ladder is a conservative default, the value that biases toward inaction, marked Default.
Rung 6 of the fallback ladder is reached when no safe default exists, the field is Missing and the mode escalates.
The conservative default is chosen to be conservative for the decision it feeds, which is field-specific and declared in the contract's field table.
A missing load forecast defaults high for peak protection, and a missing reserve price defaults low so revenue is not chased on invented prices.
The degradation design is testable by injecting quality states rather than by simulating outages.
T2 includes a degradation matrix test covering every field crossed with every quality level, asserting the mode and the risk response.
Degradation is visible in the settlement record and separable in P&L attribution.
Every field needs a declared maxStale, a fallback chain and a conservative default.
A boolean isValid per field loses the gradation that makes a proportional response possible.
Per-layer local handling of degradation produces an emergent, untested state machine.
Failing closed on everything is unoperable and erodes into ad hoc exceptions.
Three decisions are deferred on purpose, and nothing in the current design depends on any of them because every document references the abstraction rather than the choice.
The intended MILP solver is Gurobi, deferred until the Planner formulation is concrete.

Before the solver decision can be taken, the exact MILP must be specified: variable count, binary count by source, which PWL terms are General curvature, whether the simultaneity binary is enabled, and the scenario count from ADR-005 tuning.
Solver choice should follow from a benchmark on the real model rather than precede it.
The solver decision is blocked by L3-planner reaching a fixed formulation.
The solver choice changes nothing structural, because IOptimizationBackend exists precisely so it is a configuration decision.
Backends must in any case be conformance-tested against each other, and the LP-relaxation backend is needed regardless for the Tier-2 bound.
If Gurobi is confirmed, licence seat count becomes a backtest throughput constraint rather than a runtime one, because parallel backtests each need a seat.
The per-tick latency budget is deferred until operational requirements per market are settled.
Before the latency budget can be set, it must be decided whether the engine participates in continuous intraday by periodic re-optimisation on a timer or by event-driven response to book updates.
Periodic re-optimisation and event-driven response imply latency budgets two orders of magnitude apart.
The latency budget determines which tier of the co-optimisation ladder is the production path and the escalation thresholds, but not the architecture.
The tier ladder exists to make the latency-budget decision late and reversible.
Solve time distribution per tier and per gate type, as a function of scenario count and breakpoint count, is instrumented now so the latency decision is evidenced.
Intraday fill-model fidelity is deferred until the existing simulator's behaviour is characterised.

Because Execution is fixed and pre-existing and the engine's question is only which limit orders to submit, the fill model's job is to predict the simulator's behaviour and its accuracy target is defined by that rather than by the real market in the abstract.
Predicting the simulator is a narrower and much more tractable problem than a general LOB model, which is why the fill-fidelity decision can wait.
Before the fill-fidelity decision can be taken, a characterisation run against the simulator must measure realised versus predicted fill rate by price band, product and time-to-gate.

The fill-fidelity decision changes the representation of FillProbView's BoundTerm — a scalar volume cap versus a per-price-band cap — and how much of the cold tier must hold raw order-book data, but not the C2 contract shape.
Whatever is calibrated against the simulator inherits the simulator's biases.
When the engine is pointed at a real venue the fill model must be recalibrated, and the gap between simulator-calibrated and venue-calibrated behaviour becomes a named risk.

At each workstream boundary the open-decision register is reviewed for whether the blocking condition is met, whether the decision is still safely deferrable, and whether new design work has accidentally created a dependency on it.
A deferred decision that has quietly acquired dependents must be taken immediately or the dependency removed.

Available PV routinely exceeds load plus charge headroom plus the export limit, so a bridge without a curtailment term is an equality over non-negative quantities that is infeasible under an ordinary condition.
q is not merely a feasibility slack: under the Abgrenzungsoption it moves Z1NE¼ and therefore (2)¼, (23)¼ and every monthly aggregate downstream — (11), (13), (16), (30) and (32).
Whether curtailing a quarter-hour pays depends jointly on the spot price, on AW that hour, and on the state of the calendar-month aggregates.
q[t,k] is a decision variable of the Planner's MILP, priced against the same objective as every other lever.
No rule, heuristic or preprocessing step may fix q.
Valuation may publish BoundTerms constraining q to the physically available generation, but never a schedule for it.
With q as a decision variable the generation allocation is always feasible, and the export limit's shadow price becomes readable instead of implicit in an infeasibility.
Curtailment couples to the monthly aggregates (16) and (32), so horizon truncation is economically load-bearing.
A quarter-hour of q is valued only through the calendar month it falls in, so V(SOC) plus the carried monthly state must span that boundary.
Because off-take is not a control, q and the battery are the only levers on Z1NB¼ and Z1NE¼, so their joint treatment is mandatory rather than optional.

Curtailing only when the export limit binds ignores price and AW: it forgoes curtailment that pays at negative prices and forces curtailment that does not pay whenever charging could absorb the excess more cheaply.
The claim that curtailment is dominated under the delineation regime is false, because it assumes off-take is a control and that AW>0 accounting is local, and neither holds.
Curtailment as a Belief-side adjustment to pv_avail hides a decision inside a forecast, makes it unattributable in Settlement, and breaks replay.
